v1.task: Plan the library story. Write the Audience, then Frame 1, Frame 2 and Frame 3, each with what we see, the feeling and a short caption, and name the Visual detail that stays the same. In your reasoning box, explain why you ordered the frames this way. Hands-on completion: Create three finished rough frames on paper or in a free design tool. Hide the captions and check whether the visual change is readable; redraw or reorder one frame. Submit the actual frame content and the change observed. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
v1.question: Three library pictures show an exam hall, a cricket match and a bookshelf. They feel unrelated. What makes one clear story?
options: Add more unrelated attractive pictures.
Make every picture use a different audience.
Show a problem, a change and an invitation, linked by a repeated detail.
Keep the order random and explain everything later.
v1.explanation: Viewers need to see how one picture leads to the next. A repeated person or object helps connect them.

fields.label: Audience
fields.hint: Name one specific group, such as college students near the library, not everyone.
fields.prompt: Who should understand these pictures?

fields.label: Frame 1
fields.hint: What we see, the feeling, and a short caption. Show the relatable problem.
fields.prompt: What do we see in the first picture?

fields.label: Frame 2
fields.hint: What we see, the feeling, and a short caption. Show the change happening.
fields.prompt: What changes in the second picture?

fields.label: Frame 3
fields.hint: What we see, the feeling, and a caption that ends with one clear invitation.
fields.prompt: What do we see or do in the last picture?

fields.label: Visual detail that stays the same
fields.hint: One object, colour or place that appears in all three frames.
fields.prompt: Which person, object or detail links all three pictures?

link.label: Image, board or slide link (optional)
link.hint: Paste a link to a board or slide you made yourself.

v2.task: Write the AI brief for the three library images. Fill Subject and setting, choose Composition and Mood, name one Consistent detail, and list Two things to avoid. In your reasoning box, explain how you would check that viewers get the story. Hands-on completion: Create two consistent images from your brief using an available image tool or your own drawing. Compare the actual outputs, revise the brief and create a corrected image. Submit the work and the observed consistency fix. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
v2.question: AI gives you a different library visitor in each image and unreadable signs. What should your instructions make clear?
options: Ask only for more beautiful pictures.
Request a different person in every image.
Keep the unreadable sign because it looks detailed.
Describe the same person and repeated item each time, and add readable text separately.
v2.explanation: Describe what must stay the same. Check the actual images; add important words in a tool where you can read and edit them.

fields.label: Subject and setting
fields.hint: Who is in the image and where, in plain words. Be specific about the person and place.
fields.prompt: Who or what appears, and where are they?

fields.label: Composition
fields.hint: Pick the framing you would ask the AI for in all three images.
options: Eye-level medium shot, person in the middle third
Over-the-shoulder shot looking at the shelves
Wide shot with the person small in the room
Close-up on hands and the book
fields.prompt: Where should the main subject sit in the picture?

fields.label: Mood and light
fields.hint: Pick the mood a first-time visitor should feel.
options: Warm natural afternoon light, calm and welcoming
Soft morning light, fresh and hopeful
Cosy evening lamplight, quiet and safe
Bright airy daylight, open and friendly
fields.prompt: What should the mood and lighting feel like?

fields.label: Consistent detail
fields.hint: One item or colour repeated across all three images so they look like a set.
fields.prompt: What detail should stay the same in every image?

fields.label: Two things to avoid
fields.hint: Name two exclusions, such as text inside the image or invented endorsements, and say why each matters.
fields.prompt: What two things should the maker leave out?

link.label: Image, board or slide link (optional)
link.hint: Paste a link to a board or slide you made yourself.

v3.task: For the Pune photography club, write the Audience, choose one Feeling and one Action, then write the One-line message that joins all three. In your reasoning box, explain why you chose that feeling instead of another. Hands-on completion: Create the headline and finished rough visual for your intended audience. Show it to one willing viewer, record their actual interpretation and next action, then revise a conflicting detail. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
v3.question: A photography club wants first-year students to join a Saturday walk. Which poster line makes that invitation clear?
options: Cameras, friends, contests, workshops and everything for everyone.
First year? Join Saturday’s photo walk. No camera skills needed.
The greatest creative experience in history.
A photography club exists somewhere nearby.
v3.explanation: Name the person, activity and next step. Say if beginners are welcome.

fields.label: Audience
fields.hint: One specific group of students, not everyone in the college.
fields.prompt: Who should notice this message?

fields.label: Feeling you want
fields.hint: The main feeling the poster should create in that audience.
options: Curiosity
Belonging
Confidence
Excitement
Relief
fields.prompt: What should they feel?

fields.label: Action you want
fields.hint: The single next step you would ask for on the poster.
options: Turn up at the gate for the Saturday walk
Message the club on Instagram to reserve a spot
Fill a short sign-up form this week
Bring one friend along this Saturday
fields.prompt: What should they do next?

fields.label: One-line message
fields.hint: One line a stranger could repeat. It should carry the audience, the feeling and the action.
fields.prompt: What is your message in one sentence?

v4.task: Plan the open-mic poster. Choose a Focal point and a Main contrast, write the exact Poster headline, describe the Eye path in three steps, and name one Left out item. In your reasoning box, explain why that item was cut. Hands-on completion: Create and export a poster. Open it at phone size for five seconds, record what you noticed first and revise the hierarchy. Submit the finished copy, layout and before/after change. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
v4.question: An event poster gives every photo, date and logo the same size. People cannot tell what it is for. What should change?
options: Make every detail larger.
Add more photos and sponsor names.
Make the main event message stand out and reduce less important details.
Remove the event name and date.
v4.explanation: Use size and space to show what matters first. Keep the key details easy to find.

fields.label: Focal point
fields.hint: Choose the main message, person or object the viewer should notice first.
options: A large microphone image in the upper third
The bold words “Open Mic Friday” as the headline
A single performer silhouette on a dark background
The date and time set in very large numbers
fields.prompt: What should people notice first on the poster?

fields.label: Main contrast
fields.hint: Choose the main size, colour or brightness difference that makes it stand out.
options: Size: much bigger than everything else
Light against dark
One bright colour on a calm background
Empty space around it
fields.prompt: How will size or light and dark make it stand out?

fields.label: Poster headline
fields.hint: Write a short headline that makes the event clear.
fields.prompt: What is the main poster headline?

fields.label: Eye path
fields.hint: Describe three reading steps: what the viewer sees first, second and third, and where each detail sits.
fields.prompt: What should the viewer read first, second and third?

fields.label: Left out
fields.hint: Name a detail you removed so the important message has room.
fields.prompt: What will you leave out to keep the poster clear?

link.label: Image, board or slide link (optional)
link.hint: Paste a link to a board or slide you made yourself.

v5.task: Plan the book-donation flyer for readers with weak eyesight. Choose Text and background, Headline size and Colour roles, then write how a Date cue works without colour. In your reasoning box, explain how you would test it in greyscale. Hands-on completion: Create a real sample slide with your chosen type and colours. Export it, view it on a phone and in greyscale, and fix unreadable text or colour-only meaning. Submit the actual settings and observed correction. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
checks: Pick a text and background pair
Add a cue that does not rely on colour
v5.question: A flyer’s orange headline on pink disappears when printed in black and white. What helps?
options: Use dark text on a clearly lighter background.
Choose two equally light colours.
Make the text smaller.
Rely only on colour to show the important information.
v5.explanation: Text needs a clear light-dark difference to stay readable without colour.

fields.label: Text and background
fields.hint: Choose text and background colours with a clear light-dark difference.
options: Black text on white paper
Deep brown text on cream paper
White text on dark navy
Dark green text on pale yellow
fields.prompt: What text and background colours will keep the words readable?

fields.label: Headline size on A4 print
fields.hint: Choose a headline size you can read in the actual A4 print or export.
options: 36 pt
48 pt
60 pt
72 pt, only a short headline
fields.prompt: How large will the headline be on an A4 page?

fields.label: Colour roles
fields.hint: List your colours and what each marks, such as headings or warnings.
options: Two: one for text, one for background
Three: text, background and one accent for the date
Three: dark text, light background and a warm band for the title
Four: text, background, accent and a soft highlight
fields.prompt: What job does each colour have?

fields.label: Date cue without colour
fields.hint: Use words, a shape or placement so the date remains clear in black and white.
fields.prompt: How will you show the date clearly without relying on colour?

link.label: Image, board or slide link (optional)
link.hint: Paste a link to a board or slide you made yourself.

v6.task: Turn the library’s 420, 510 and 640 into one honest chart story. Choose the Chart type, write a Headline finding, a Caption of under 25 words, and one thing the numbers do not prove. In your reasoning box, explain why that chart fits. Hands-on completion: Create the chart from the supplied numbers in a spreadsheet or chart tool. Change one value and confirm that the chart updates. Submit the data, chart labels, caption and observed correction to a misleading choice. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
checks: State the finding in a headline
Keep the caption short and accurate
Name something the data does not prove
v6.question: Library visits rise from 420 to 640. A bar chart starts at 400 and makes the rise look huge. What is misleading?
options: The labels show actual visit counts.
The chart includes both months.
The chart has a title.
The bars exaggerate the change because their scale does not start at zero.
v6.explanation: Bar lengths should represent the numbers fairly. Starting at zero stops a modest rise from looking many times larger.

fields.label: Chart type
fields.hint: Choose the simplest chart that clearly shows the change over the three supplied months.
options: Bar chart starting at zero
Line chart with three labelled points
Big-number callout with a small arrow
Column chart with value labels on each column
fields.prompt: Which chart will you use to show these numbers?

fields.label: Headline finding
fields.hint: Write one finding supported by the actual numbers, without exaggerating.
fields.prompt: What one finding does the chart show?

fields.label: Caption
fields.hint: Use fewer than 25 words. State only what the numbers show, including the period and units where needed.
fields.prompt: What will your chart caption explain?

fields.label: What the numbers do not prove
fields.hint: Explain one conclusion the data cannot support, such as why visits changed.
fields.prompt: What can these numbers not tell you?

link.label: Image, board or slide link (optional)
link.hint: Paste a link to a board or slide you made yourself.

v7.task: Plan the bakery’s five-slide carousel with one idea per slide. Write one short line and a picture note for Slide 1 hook, Slides 2 and 3 build, Slide 4 proof and Slide 5 invitation. In your reasoning box, name one claim to check before posting. Hands-on completion: Create and export five carousel slides. Read the export on a phone, remove a repeated idea and revise the final action. Submit the actual slide copy, sequence and the problem you corrected. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
v7.question: One bakery slide lists ingredients, delivery, a discount and health claims. It is hard to read. What helps?
options: Add more words in smaller text.
Repeat all the details on every slide.
Keep one main idea on this slide and move other ideas to separate slides.
Remove the final order instruction from the whole sequence.
v7.explanation: Give each slide one clear job. Readers should be able to follow the message and next step.

fields.label: Slide 1: hook
fields.hint: One line and a picture note that stops the scroll. A question or surprise works better than a logo.
fields.prompt: How will the first slide catch attention?

fields.label: Slide 2: build
fields.hint: One line and a picture note: the first idea that adds interest.
fields.prompt: What one idea will the second slide add?

fields.label: Slide 3: build
fields.hint: One line and a picture note: a second, different idea.
fields.prompt: What one new idea will the third slide add?

fields.label: Slide 4: proof
fields.hint: One line and a picture note that makes the claim believable.
fields.prompt: What fact or real example supports your message?

fields.label: Slide 5: invitation
fields.hint: One line and a picture note with a single action, such as ordering the six-cookie box for ₹240.
fields.prompt: What should the viewer do after the last slide?

link.label: Image, board or slide link (optional)
link.hint: Paste a link to a board or slide you made yourself.

v8.task: Review the imagined lunch-box image. Write one finding each for Hands and text, Bias or gaps and Consent or rights, choose a Verdict, then write the Revision request. In your reasoning box, explain why you chose that verdict. Hands-on completion: Inspect an actual image you made or may use, not just its description. Create a corrected image or replace it with your own work. Submit the observed defects, rights check and actual before/after change. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
checks: Note a hands or text defect
v8.question: An AI banner for a tea stall closely copies a famous actor’s face without permission. What should happen before printing?
options: Print it because AI made it.
Replace or change the face so it does not copy the person, then check the image again.
Hide a small corner but keep the recognisable face.
Say the actor supports the tea stall.
v8.explanation: AI-made images still need careful checks. Do not imply a real person’s involvement or permission when you do not have it.

fields.label: Hands and text finding
fields.hint: Look at the actual image. Note visible problems such as extra fingers or unreadable words.
fields.prompt: What mistakes can you see in the hands or words?

fields.label: Bias or gaps finding
fields.hint: Check whether people are missing, stereotyped or shown unfairly. Describe what you see.
fields.prompt: Who or what is missing or shown unfairly?

fields.label: Consent or rights finding
fields.hint: Check faces, logos and source material. Do not assume AI output comes with permission.
fields.prompt: Do you have permission to use the people and material shown?

fields.label: Verdict
fields.hint: Choose use, revise or replace based on the checks you actually made.
options: Use as it is
Use after fixing small details in the layout
Regenerate with a new prompt
Reject it and use a real photo
fields.prompt: Is the image ready to use, or must it change?

fields.label: Revision request
fields.hint: Ask for specific changes to the visible problems. Then check the new image too.
fields.prompt: What exactly should be fixed in the next version?

link.label: Image, board or slide link (optional)
link.hint: Paste a link to a board or slide you made yourself.

v9.task: Plan the three-slide pitch for the bicycle repair stall. Write the Problem slide, the Insight slide and the Ask slide, with a headline and picture for each, and choose the Proof for the insight. In your reasoning box, explain how this order helps persuade the council. Hands-on completion: Create and export three pitch slides, then record a one-minute presentation. Watch it back, correct an unsupported claim or unclear transition and update the slides. Submit actual slide copy and recording timecodes. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
checks: Write a headline for each slide
Make the problem easy to feel
v9.question: Students start a pitch by asking for ₹12,000. The listeners ask why the project is needed. What should the students explain first?
options: The problem, what they learned, and why their idea would help.
A larger amount of money with no explanation.
Only the colours used on the slides.
A promise that the idea can never fail.
v9.explanation: Show the need and supporting facts before asking for help. Then the request has a clear reason.

fields.label: Problem slide
fields.hint: Show who has the problem and what is difficult for them.
fields.prompt: What problem will your first slide show?

fields.label: Insight slide
fields.hint: State the useful idea you learned from what you observed.
fields.prompt: What have you learned that helps explain the problem?

fields.label: Proof for the insight
fields.hint: Use a real fact, observation or example. Do not invent evidence.
options: A quick survey of 30 hostel students
A photo count of bicycles with small faults
A comparison of repair shop prices
A short quote from a hostel warden
fields.prompt: What fact or example supports that idea?

fields.label: Ask slide
fields.hint: Say what help you need, what it will be used for, and the next step.
fields.prompt: What help or action will you ask for on the last slide?

link.label: Image, board or slide link (optional)
link.hint: Paste a link to a board or slide you made yourself.

v10.task: Storyboard the Jaipur tutoring-volunteer campaign. Name the Audience and repeating detail, write Frames 1 to 3 and Frames 4 and 5 with a caption each, choose the Risk and fix, and write an AI disclosure line. In your reasoning box, explain why the order of frames works. Hands-on completion: Create and export five campaign frames using your earlier work. View the full sequence on a phone, record where its message breaks and revise that frame. Submit the actual frame content and before/after correction. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
v10.question: Five pictures in one campaign use different characters and colours. People do not see a connection. What should stay the same?
options: A new audience and goal in every picture.
Unrelated characters with no connection.
Different messages that point to unrelated actions.
One repeated detail and a shared colour scheme across all five pictures.
v10.explanation: Repeated details help people recognise one connected campaign. Keep its audience and next step consistent too.

fields.label: Audience and repeating detail
fields.hint: Who the campaign speaks to, and the one object or colour that repeats in every frame.
fields.prompt: Who are the pictures for, and what detail links them?

fields.label: Frames 1 to 3
fields.hint: One line each: what we see, plus a short caption. Start with the problem and build to the change.
fields.prompt: What will the first three pictures show?

fields.label: Frames 4 and 5
fields.hint: One line each: what we see and a caption. Frame 5 ends with the invitation to volunteer.
fields.prompt: What will the last two pictures show?

fields.label: Risk and fix
fields.hint: Pick the pair you would act on for this campaign.
options: Real children may appear, so use drawn illustrations instead of photos
AI faces may look odd, so edit them by hand before posting
Captions may be misread, so test them with three college students
Images may copy an artist’s style, so avoid naming artists in prompts
fields.prompt: What might confuse viewers, and how will you fix it?

fields.label: AI disclosure line
fields.hint: A short plain line telling viewers that some images were made with AI.
fields.prompt: How will you tell viewers which parts used AI?

link.label: Image, board or slide link (optional)
link.hint: Paste a link to a board or slide you made yourself.
